Chapter 2: The Myth of Progress and the Denial of Harm
Have you ever noticed how people love to say, "Things are always getting better"? It’s almost comforting, isn’t it? We hear it everywhere—from classrooms to campaign speeches, and even in casual conversations about the past. There’s this idea that each new generation is smarter, kinder, and more enlightened than the last. That the big problems—like sexism and racism—are mostly behind us.
But here’s the thing: for a lot of people, that story just doesn’t match their reality.
Imagine a young woman, just out of college, walking into her very first job. She’s excited, full of hope, and ready to show what she can do. But it doesn’t take long before she starts noticing the little things. Maybe her ideas get brushed aside until someone else repeats them. Or maybe there are jokes that make her uncomfortable, and promotions that always seem to go to the same type of people. And when she speaks up? She’s met with, “That’s just how it is. Things are better than they used to be.”
That right there is the myth of progress in action. It’s the idea that if things have improved a little, we should just be grateful and stop asking for more. “At least you can vote now,” someone might say, as if that fixes everything. The real message? Don’t complain. Trust that things will keep getting better on their own.
But progress isn’t automatic. It’s not some natural law that just moves forward by itself. Progress takes effort—it happens because people demand it, fight for it, and sometimes pay a really heavy price. Believing that things always get better on their own? Well, that’s just an excuse to avoid the hard work of real change. It lets those with power ignore the harm that’s still happening, and pretend that the struggle is over.
And this denial? It pops up everywhere—not just in the big stuff. Think about the way people talk about old movies, or music, or even offhand jokes. When someone points out a problem—a sexist joke in a classic film, for example—the reaction is often defensive. “It was a different time,” people say. Or, “Don’t be so sensitive.” The underlying story is always the same: the past was bad, but now everything’s fine.
But let’s be honest—culture doesn’t magically change just because time goes by. Harmful ideas stick around, often in ways that are hard to see. Maybe a parent laughs at a joke on TV, not realizing their kid is soaking up what’s considered normal. Or a group of friends tells a story about a “crazy ex-girlfriend,” without noticing how it shapes everyone’s view of women. These habits might seem harmless, but they’re actually the foundation of much bigger problems.
Here’s something worth thinking about: Most of us want to believe we’d be heroes if we lived in the past. That we would’ve spoken up, or stood on the right side of history. But the real challenge isn’t about what we might have done back then. It’s about what we’re willing to do right now. It’s easy to judge the obvious villains of history. It’s much tougher to notice when those same patterns are playing out in our own lives.
The myth of progress is so tempting because it offers an easy out. It whispers, “You’ve done enough. No need to push any further.” But real change? That takes more than good intentions. It means really listening, paying attention, and being brave enough to question the stories that make us comfortable.
Sometimes, making a difference starts with a simple question. When someone says, “Things are better now,” ask yourself—better for who? Who’s still being left out? Who’s paying the price for someone else’s comfort? These aren’t easy questions, but they’re the ones that actually matter.
In the end, denying harm isn’t just about ignoring the past—it’s about not seeing what’s happening right in front of us. It’s a way to protect the stories we like, even when those stories hurt others. But if we really want to move forward, we have to face what’s real, not just what feels reassuring.
